name: Segment Anything Model (SAM / SAM2) zero-shot prompted segmentation

identity.method_name: Segment Anything Model (SAM) and Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), applied zero-shot with point/box prompts, typically via the segment-geospatial (samgeo) geospatial wrapper
identity.core_idea: SAM/SAM2 are transformer-based promptable segmentation foundation models: a large ViT (SAM) or Hiera (SAM2) image encoder produces a dense image embedding once per image, and a lightweight prompt encoder plus mask decoder then turns a point, box, or mask prompt into an instance mask in real time, without any task-specific training. The geospatial community (via the segment-geospatial/samgeo package) wraps this for satellite rasters by chipping large scenes into tiles, running SAM/SAM2 per tile, and georeferencing the returned masks back onto the map. Critically, SAM returns an unlabelled 'this is one coherent region' mask, not a semantic class -- a human or a downstream rule still has to decide whether a given mask is 'water,' 'hyacinth,' 'bare bed,' or 'built-up.'
identity.official_dataset_ids: SA-1B (SAM's training image/mask corpus, released by Meta AI, CC BY 4.0 licence, no formal geospatial catalog ID) and SA-V (SAM2's video training corpus, also CC BY 4.0). Neither dataset contains satellite or aerial remote-sensing imagery -- both are natural, ground-level and web-sourced photographs and videos. This is itself the central domain-shift flag for this item: the model has never seen Sentinel-2 imagery, hyacinth mats, or lake shorelines during training.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Zero-shot foundation model. Literally no training labels are required at all, which is the exact reason this item is included as 'the hardest constraint in this project' solved by construction. The real cost is displaced, not eliminated: it moves from a labelling budget into a prompt-engineering and post-hoc semantic-assignment budget -- a human still decides where to click (or draw a box) per lake per year, and still decides what class name to attach to each returned mask.
fit_to_project.input_required: SAM's image encoder expects an ordinary 3-channel image (RGB or a pseudo-RGB false-colour composite), because it was trained exclusively on natural photographs. The project's 6-band (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL) 20 m cube would have to be reduced to a 3-band composite per scene before SAM can be run at all -- unlike A1 (uses the full stack) and A2 (uses 6 bands including SWIR), this method structurally discards most of the project's spectral information, including the SWIR band the project's own MNDWI baseline depends on.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes, in the narrow sense that SAM is never locally fit, so the 42-lake-year sample size is irrelevant to model fitting. But the real unit of work at inference is one prompted image per lake-year (with a handful of point/box prompts each), i.e. 42 independent, manually-driven prompting decisions -- not '42 training samples' in any statistical sense, and not something that benefits from more data the way a trained model would.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- this is the item's stated, defining advantage, and it holds: no pixel-level or patch-level label set of any kind is required to run SAM/SAM2.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: The concept of 'resolution match' does not really apply to SAM/SAM2 the way it does to a sensor-calibrated model, because both were trained on arbitrary-resolution web photographs with no defined ground sampling distance -- but this is itself the problem, not a reassurance. At 20 m/pixel, the project's smallest lake (Sankey Tank, ~12.4 ha, roughly 310 total pixels, i.e. about an 18x18-pixel patch) renders as a tiny, low-texture blob with almost none of the edge, shading, and object-boundary cues SAM's encoder was trained to exploit on macroscopic natural objects (cars, animals, furniture, people). This is a more severe mismatch in practice than a simple resolution gap, because it is a mismatch in visual grammar, not just scale. Published geospatial SAM successes that report strong point-prompt performance (e.g. lake-shoreline segmentation at 0.45 m resolution [verify]) are drawn from imagery roughly 40x finer than the project's grid.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None for the model weights themselves. A light manual step is still required at inference time: a human places prompts per lake-year and assigns a semantic class (water / hyacinth / bare bed / built-up) to each returned mask, since SAM has no notion of these classes.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four directly. Does not add rows to the 42-row table, does not touch the static OpenStreetMap-buildings problem, does not manufacture real ground truth (an unverified SAM mask is not ground truth, it is another unverified guess, arguably a noisier one than the project's own MNDWI baseline given the RGB-only input), and does not add extra scenes per year.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. SAM segments 'a coherent region in one static image'; it has no temporal state and no semantic understanding of dredging, silt, or fill. Telling apart a drained-for-desilting bare patch from an encroached, permanently-filled patch requires comparing across years and requires domain knowledge SAM does not have -- any such logic has to be built entirely outside SAM, applied to a sequence of SAM's single-date masks.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: This is the item's hardest and most clearly negative case, and the project's own framing correctly anticipates it. Water hyacinth mats have amorphous, gradient, diffuse boundaries (patchy floating clusters with no crisp edge against open water), which is the opposite of the well-defined, closed-contour natural objects SAM was trained on. The expected failure mode is over-segmentation -- a single hyacinth mat fragmenting into many small disconnected masks -- or, depending on where a prompt lands, under-segmentation that merges hyacinth with adjacent open water or shoreline vegetation into one mask. General remote-sensing SAM literature confirms over-segmentation on heterogeneous, low-boundary-contrast scenes as a known, recurring failure mode of zero-shot point-prompted SAM [general finding from Osco et al. 2023 and related geospatial-SAM literature; the specific hyacinth case was not directly tested in any located primary source and should be treated as an informed extrapolation, marked verify].
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None -- SAM's output is an arbitrary-shaped mask with no inherent link to any cadastral or legal reference; whatever georeferencing exists comes entirely from the samgeo wrapper mapping pixel coordinates back to the scene's known CRS, exactly as for any other raster method, and still requires a separately-chosen boundary/buffer layer (OpenStreetMap proxy or an authoritative source) to become legally meaningful.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: In principle each year could be re-prompted independently, so the derived output could vary year to year -- but this cuts both ways: re-prompting every year introduces prompt-placement drift as an artificial source of year-to-year variation that has nothing to do with the lake itself, which is a genuine risk of manufacturing spurious 'change' purely from inconsistent manual prompting, not from anything that happened on the ground.

implementation.libraries: segment-anything (github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything, Apache-2.0) or sam2 (github.com/facebookresearch/sam2, Apache-2.0); segment-geospatial / samgeo (github.com/opengeos/segment-geospatial, MIT license) for raster chipping, coordinate-aware prompt helpers, and mask georeferencing; PyTorch as the underlying backend for both model families.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Yes -- SAM ViT-B/L/H checkpoints and SAM2 (Hiera tiny/small/base-plus/large) checkpoints are released directly by Meta AI on the official repositories, trained on SA-1B (SAM) and SA-V (SAM2), which are exclusively natural-image and natural-video corpora, not remote sensing or Sentinel-2 imagery of any kind.
implementation.licence: Apache License 2.0 for both SAM and SAM2 code and model checkpoints -- confirmed directly at github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything/blob/main/LICENSE and github.com/facebookresearch/sam2/blob/main/LICENSE. This is a fully permissive licence with no restriction on academic or derivative use. The SA-1B and SA-V training datasets are CC BY 4.0, relevant only if the raw training data itself were to be used, which is not needed for inference. segment-geospatial (samgeo) is MIT-licensed. Of the three A-group items, this is the item with the clearest, most fully confirmed licensing position.
implementation.compute_requirement: GPU strongly preferred, unlike A2. SAM's ViT-H checkpoint (~2.4 GB) and SAM2's larger encoders are heavy transformer backbones; CPU inference is possible but slow per tile (potentially seconds to tens of seconds per 1024x1024 chip on CPU versus sub-second on a free-tier T4 GPU). Given the project's small scale (42 scenes, a handful of chips each), this comfortably fits within free Colab/Kaggle GPU quotas, so it remains feasible for a solo student, but it is not truly CPU-only the way A2 is.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 4-7 student-days: environment and model setup (0.5-1 day); building the raster-to-RGB-chip pipeline with samgeo, including deciding which 3 of the 6 bands to composite (0.5-1 day); iterative prompt design and placement per lake-year, expected to require several rounds given the anticipated over-segmentation on hyacinth (1-2 days); post-hoc mask-to-semantic-class assignment and visual QA (1-2 days); writeup (0.5-1 day). This sits below A1's full training pipeline and roughly on par with, or slightly above, A2's near-zero-effort inference run.

evaluation.metrics: IoU/Dice of SAM's returned mask against a manually-produced visual reference for a spot-checked subset of lake-years (again a visual audit, not a formal accuracy, since no ground truth exists); arguably more honest and more informative than a single aggregate score here is a qualitative failure catalogue -- the count and description of masks that were usably clean versus over-segmented versus under-segmented per lake-year, since the failure mode itself (not just its magnitude) is the finding that matters most for this project.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Because no local training occurs, a train/test split in the ML-fitting sense does not apply. The meaningful check instead is prompt-consistency / inter-annotator validation: have a second person independently repeat the same prompting protocol on a held-out subset of lake-years and measure agreement between the two annotators' resulting masks, since a single annotator's prompt placement is itself a subjective, non-reproducible input that this method cannot avoid.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dominant risk here is prompt leakage rather than classical data leakage: if the person placing prompts already has prior knowledge of which lakes or years are 'supposed' to show encroachment (e.g. from news coverage of Bellandur or Varthur), prompt placement can be unconsciously steered toward confirming that prior, especially since the same person repeats this judgment-based step 42 times. This risk is structurally higher for SAM than for A1/A2 precisely because SAM has no other source of decision-making besides the human prompt.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: SAM/SAM2's mask decoder does natively return 3 candidate masks per prompt along with a predicted-IoU confidence score for each -- a genuine built-in uncertainty signal, and in this narrow respect better native support than either A1 (bare softmax) or A2 (bare sigmoid/logit) out of the box. However, this predicted-IoU score is the model's own self-assessment against its training distribution of natural photographs, not a statistically calibrated interval against this project's actual imagery, and should not be over-interpreted as a true probability of correctness on Sentinel-2 lake scenes.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable -- no data augmentation or synthetic label expansion is part of this method; SAM is applied directly to real, unmodified project imagery at inference time only.

evidence.published_performance: Osco et al., 'The Segment Anything Model (SAM) for Remote Sensing Applications: From Zero to One Shot,' International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation, 2023 (ScienceDirect S1569843223003643; arXiv 2306.16623), reports strong zero-shot performance on crisp, well-bounded remote-sensing targets (buildings, roads, agricultural field boundaries) but reduced performance on irregular or heterogeneous natural targets under prompted zero-shot segmentation [verify -- exact IoU/accuracy figures per target type were not independently retrieved from primary full text in this session]. A separate finding located in this research states that point prompts proved highly effective for segmenting lakes at 0.45 m resolution [verify -- source and exact metric not independently confirmed]; this resolution is roughly 40x finer than the project's 20 m grid and is not a comparable regime. No published, primary-source-confirmed accuracy number was located specifically for water hyacinth or other floating-macrophyte segmentation with SAM/SAM2 at any resolution.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: The located remote-sensing SAM evaluations are global, mixed-target benchmark studies (buildings, crops, general land cover, various sensors and resolutions), not lake water bodies specifically and not tropical hyacinth-infested lakes; several of the strongest reported geospatial SAM successes are on sub-metre aerial or very-high-resolution commercial imagery, a resolution class the project does not have and cannot obtain within its current data pipeline.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No published SAM or SAM2 application was found for Bengaluru lakes, other Indian urban lakes, or water hyacinth specifically. This is a complete evidence gap, not merely a thin one.
evidence.evidence_recency: SAM: April 2023. SAM2: 2024. The general remote-sensing SAM review and application literature spans 2023-2025 and is genuinely recent, but its positive results are concentrated on crisp targets at sub-metre resolution -- a materially different regime from this project's amorphous vegetation targets at 20 m, so recency of the surrounding literature does not translate into recency of directly applicable evidence.
evidence.primary_sources: SAM repository: https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything. SAM2 repository: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam2 ; SAM2 paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2408.00714v1 ('SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos'). segment-geospatial (samgeo): https://github.com/opengeos/segment-geospatial and https://samgeo.gishub.org/. Osco et al. 2023: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jag.2023.103540 ; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1569843223003643 ; arXiv preprint: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.16623. Meta AI SAM2 announcement: https://ai.meta.com/blog/segment-anything-2/.

risk.failure_modes: Over-segmentation of hyacinth mats into disconnected fragments (the stated hardest case, and the item's central expected failure); the smallest lakes (Sankey Tank, ~18x18 pixels at 20 m) may be too low-resolution and low-texture for SAM's encoder to return a meaningful proposal of any kind, independent of prompt quality; heavy reliance on per-lake-year manual prompt placement introduces annotator-dependent variance that is difficult to report honestly as a 'model accuracy' rather than a mixture of model behaviour and human judgement; the mandatory reduction to an RGB-only or pseudo-RGB composite discards the SWIR band that the project's own MNDWI baseline is built on, meaning SAM cannot, even in principle, reproduce the physical water-index logic the rest of the project relies on.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask directly: 'you said no labels were needed, but you personally clicked a point or drew a box on each of 42 images -- isn't that still a human-supplied label, just moved to inference time?' This is a fair and largely unanswerable objection that must be conceded plainly: SAM removes the need for a training label set, but it does not remove the need for a human decision at inference time, and that decision is exactly where prior belief about 'which lakes look encroached' can re-enter the analysis through the back door. A panel is also likely to ask why an RGB-only foundation model was used on a project whose own baseline method depends on a SWIR-based index.
risk.honest_expectation: A genuinely useful exploratory tool for a first qualitative look at lake shorelines, and a legitimate way to demonstrate that the student explored the current zero-label foundation-model frontier as an option -- but not a credible replacement for the project's water/hyacinth/built-up quantification pipeline, given the RGB-only input, the expected amorphous-boundary over-segmentation on exactly the hyacinth confound the project cares about most, and the resolution/texture mismatch on the smallest lakes. Expect a mostly null-to-modest result if judged by any IoU-style metric against a reference mask, and treat this item's real value as a documented feasibility-and-failure-mode case study for the report, not as a production component of the final pipeline.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject as the project's primary deep-learning deliverable; consider-with-reasons as a one-off qualitative exploration or a figure in the final report. The zero-label appeal is real and the licence position is the cleanest of the three A-group items, but the mandatory RGB-only input (discarding the SWIR band the baseline depends on), the expected amorphous-boundary over-segmentation on water hyacinth specifically, and the small-lake resolution/texture mismatch make it unsuitable to carry the guide's 'one deep learning model' requirement; A1 (a U-Net trained on the project's own multispectral bands, with a dedicated hyacinth class) is the better-fitted option for that role.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We tested SAM/SAM2 zero-shot on lake imagery to see whether we could avoid labelling entirely, but it requires RGB-only input (dropping the SWIR band our water index depends on), is expected to over-segment the amorphous hyacinth mats we most need to isolate, and still requires a human to place a prompt on every lake in every year -- so we report it as an exploratory feasibility check, not as the project's deep-learning model.
